faq.q: Why does writing a worry down help?
faq.a: When a worry is on paper, it stops spinning around your head and you can look at it calmly. Many people find it feels smaller once it is written down.
asks: Should I write my worries down?

faq.q: How do I check if a worry is true?
faq.a: Ask yourself: what has happened before? What would I tell a friend with this worry? What is most likely to happen? Worries are guesses, not facts.
asks: How do I know if my worry is real?

faq.q: What if I cannot fix my worry?
faq.a: Some things are out of your control, like the weather. Then you can do a calming thing, talk to someone, and gently let the worry float by.
asks: What do I do with worries I cannot change?

faq.a: Worry time is a short, set time each day, about ten minutes, to think about your worries. If a worry pops up at other times, you tell it, "I will think about you at worry time."

faq.q: What if my worry is about something serious?
faq.a: If you feel unsafe, someone is hurting you, or something at home or school is really wrong, tell a trusted grown-up straight away, like a parent, a teacher or a school counsellor.
asks: Who do I tell about a big worry?

facts: Worry dolls from Guatemala are tiny handmade dolls that children tell their worries to before bed, a tradition now known worldwide.
Setting aside a short daily "worry time" is a technique psychologists use to stop worries filling the whole day.

quiz.say: If you cannot fix a worry, what can you do?

options.show: Do a calming thing and let it float by
options.say: Do a calming thing and let it float by

quiz.why: For things out of your control, calming yourself and letting the worry pass works best.

wrong.0: Keeping worries secret usually makes them feel bigger.
wrong.2: Thinking about it all night makes worry grow and stops you sleeping.

quiz.say: Why is it useful to check the facts about a worry?
quiz.show: Why is it useful to check the facts about a worry?

options.show: Worries often guess the worst, so facts can shrink them
options.say: Worries often guess the worst, so facts can shrink them

quiz.why: Checking what really happened before shows that most worries are much bigger than reality.

wrong.1: Facts usually show the worry is less likely than it felt.
wrong.2: Facts help a lot, because worries are guesses.
